summary: For 7\u20138 year olds comparing engineering solutions that slow or prevent wind and [curriculum wording omitted; reference 2-ESS2-1]. The core target is COMPARING two or three solutions (plants/ground cover, barriers/walls, windbreaks) against EVIDENCE from a simple fair test \u2014 not opinion \u2014 and defending a claim about which works best, while recognising trade-offs and that the best choice depends on the situation.
misconceptions: 'One solution is always best' — not seeing that the right choice depends on the situation and trade-offs.
'Plants cause erosion / plants are just decoration' — not recognising roots bind and hold soil.
'Walls stop all erosion forever' — overlooking that barriers can fail, overtop, or shift.
'You can just decide which is best by looking' — skipping the fair test/evidence.
'Wind and water erosion need the same solution' — windbreaks vs water barriers suit different agents.

activities.title: Erosion-defence fair test: bare vs planted vs walled
steps: First watch or recall how wind and water carry soil away from a slope, so the solutions have a clear purpose.

Set up three identical sloped trays of soil: one bare, one covered with living ground cover such as grass/moss (the cover shields the soil surface and roots, where present, bind it), one backed by a small retaining wall.
Pour the SAME amount of water from the SAME height over each tray, and catch the runoff/soil in a tray beneath each.

Measure or compare how much soil each slope lost (e.g. read a soil-loss catch tray or meter) and rank the three trays from least to most soil lost, using the bare tray as the no-protection comparison.
Name which solution worked best and point to the evidence you saw or measured to justify it.
State what you kept the same (water amount, pour height, slope) to make it a fair test.
Design and drop in your OWN barrier and test it the same way.
activities.insight: You judge which solution works best from evidence in a fair comparative test \u2014 keeping everything the same except the solution \u2014 rather than deciding by belief or by guessing from how a solution looks before testing.

activities.title: Which solution for THIS situation? Surfacing trade-offs
steps: Compare a rainy slope scenario with a windy flat field scenario.

Decide which solution suits each situation: e.g. a windbreak (hedge/fence) to slow wind on the flat field, or a wall on a water slope \u2014 noting that plants/ground cover help reduce BOTH wind and water erosion because their roots bind the soil and the cover shields the surface.
Explain why one solution can beat another when the situation changes (water pooling/overtopping a wall, roots binding soil, wind vs water).
Consider cost/effort trade-offs for a site (e.g. 'the wall costs more \u2014 is it worth it here?') and justify your pick.
activities.insight: There is rarely one perfect solution: the best choice depends on the situation (slope vs flat, wind vs water, cost/effort), and solutions have trade-offs; some solutions (like ground cover/plants) can help against more than one agent.

activities.title: Reading and organising the comparison evidence
steps: Match each solution to how it helps (plants/roots \u2192 bind and hold soil, and the cover shields the surface; wall/terrace \u2192 block or hold back soil and water; windbreak \u2192 slow the wind).
Sort solutions by which eroding agent(s) they suit, remembering some solutions help against more than one.
Read a results chart (solution \u2192 how it helps \u2192 how much soil lost) and identify which slope lost the least soil.
Build a comparison chart from your own test results and use it to defend your claim.
activities.insight: Organising results into a comparison (solution \u2192 mechanism \u2192 how well it worked) lets you reason clearly about which solution wins and why.

checkQuestion: Here are three trays of sloped soil, plus pieces of grass/moss, a small wall, and a bare tray. Pour the same cup of water over each from the same height, then tell me which lost the least soil and use what you saw to say which solution works best and why.
checkAnswer: The child pours equally over each tray, observes that the bare soil washes away most while the planted or walled slopes hold more soil, and concludes which solution worked best — citing what they saw and having kept the water amount and height the same (a fair test).
